raw_segments.text: When a carpenter is ill, he asks the physician for a rough and ready cure—an emetic or
a purge or a cottery or the knife—these are his remedies.
And if someone prescribes for him a course of dietetics, and tells him that he must swathe
and swaddle his head, and all that sort of thing, he replies at once that he has no time
to be ill, and that he sees no good in a life which is spent in nursing his disease to the
And therefore bidding good-bye to this sort of physician, he resumes his ordinary habits,
and either gets well and lives and does his business, or, if his constitution fails, he
dies and has no more trouble.
